html:
The euro is the shared currency of most countries of the European Union, launched on 1 January 1999 by eleven countries. At first it existed only in bank accounts and markets. Euro notes and coins came into people's hands on 1 January 2002, replacing old currencies such as the Deutsche Mark, the French franc and the Italian lira.

The idea grew out of the long project of European unity that began with the Treaty of Rome in 1957. The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 set the rules: countries had to keep inflation, debt and deficits low to join. The European Central Bank in Frankfurt sets interest rates for the whole zone.

Supporters hoped one currency would make trade easier and tie Germany and France more closely together after centuries of war. It did make prices easy to compare and travel simpler, and it became the world's second most used currency for reserves after the US dollar.

  • Greece joined in 2001, and more countries have joined since. Today 21 of the 27 EU members use it.
  • The debt crisis from 2009 showed the weakness of one interest rate and no shared budget. Greece, Ireland, Portugal and others needed bailouts.
  • The zone survived, and the European Central Bank's promise in 2012 to do "whatever it takes" calmed the markets.
